prompt: Tell me a story in five sentences about a girl and her dog.
generations: Every morning, Mia raced her scruffy terrier Biscuit to the old oak at the end of the lane, and every morning she lost. The summer she turned ten, Biscuit's muzzle went gray and his sprints slowed to a trot, so Mia started losing on purpose without telling him. One October dawn he stopped halfway, sat in the frost, and looked back at her as if apologizing. Mia knelt, pressed her forehead to his, and whispered that the race had never been the point. They walked to the oak together after that, side by side, for every morning they had left.

The girl smelled of rain and peanut butter, and that was how I chose her at the shelter, pressing my nose through the bars until she laughed. She named me Waffle, which I found undignified and perfect. When the shouting started downstairs at night, she would climb into my crate even though she barely fit, and I would lay my head over her heart until it slowed. Years later she carried a small human home from the hospital and set it beside me, whispering that this was my job now too. I am old and my eyes are clouding, but I still know her by the rain, the peanut butter, and the way her footsteps mean home.

On Mars Colony Seven, pets were banned, so eleven-year-old Zadie built one from a decommissioned survey rover and named him Rustbucket. He couldn't bark, but he beeped in a pattern she taught him that meant I'm here, I'm here. When a dust storm knocked out the habitat's beacon and stranded Zadie's mother in the wastes, Rustbucket's old survey sensors found her heat signature through forty kilometers of red static. The council voted the next week to reclassify him from 'equipment' to 'resident.' Zadie painted a collar around his chassis anyway, just so no one would ever mistake him again.

The end: an old woman scatters ashes under an apple tree while a puppy tugs at her sleeve. Before that: a gray-faced dog sleeps through his last winter on a girl-turned-woman's wedding dress, shedding on the silk while she laughs instead of scolding. Before that: a teenager fails her driving test and cries into fur that smells like sunshine and dirt. Before that: a mutt drags a seven-year-old out of a frozen pond by her coat hood, and the town gives him a medal he immediately buries. First: a cardboard box on a porch, a note reading 'please,' and a girl who opens the flaps and falls in love.

"You can't come to school, Pepper, they have rules," Anna said, blocking the door with her backpack. "Rules," said the dog, "were written by people who never had to wait eight hours by a window." Anna dropped the backpack, because Pepper had never spoken before, not once in six years. "I only get the words on your last day needing me," Pepper said gently, "and today you're going to walk in there and make a friend, a real one, and I wanted to say I'm proud." Anna made the friend, and that evening Pepper just barked like always, but he barked it like a secret they both kept.

After the cities went quiet, June and her shepherd mix, Ash, walked north following the geese, because her father had said geese always know where the living things are. Ash caught rabbits and June read to him from a waterlogged atlas by firelight, promising him an ocean neither of them had seen. At a collapsed bridge, raiders took her pack, her knife, and her atlas, but they backed away from sixty pounds of low growl standing over her. On the ninetieth day they crested a dune and there it was, gray and roaring and endless. Ash barked at the waves like he'd personally summoned them, and June laughed for the first time since the world ended.

Sightless since birth, Priya knew the world as textures and echoes until Juno arrived, a golden retriever with a harness and infinite patience. Juno became her geometry: the pause that meant curb, the lean that meant turn, the full-body block that once meant a cyclist running a red light. In college, classmates learned that petting Juno was forbidden but talking to Priya was encouraged, which was, she said, the whole lesson in one dog. When Juno retired at ten, Priya kept her, and a young successor named Atlas took up the harness while Juno supervised from the couch. Some people have a guide dog and then a pet, Priya explained, but she preferred to say she had a professor emeritus.

You are nine, and the dog at the pound has three legs and a face like a burnt cookie, and you choose her anyway because she is the only one not begging. You name her Tripod as a joke and then feel guilty and change it to Trixie, and she forgives you the way dogs forgive everything, instantly and in full. All that year, when the kids at school call you names, you come home and tell Trixie, and she listens with her one ear up like your words are the evening news. You will not remember most of fourth grade, but you will remember the exact weight of her chin on your knee. Decades from now, choosing whom to trust, you will still measure everyone against a three-legged dog who never once begged.

The dog appeared the night Wren's grandmother died: a lean white hound sitting in the garden, visible only in moonlight and mirrors. It followed her to school as a cold spot at her heel, and it howled, silently, whenever she was about to make a mistake, like the day she almost got into a stranger's car. Wren finally found the photograph in her grandmother's attic, a girl in 1953 with the same white hound and the words 'Guardian - passed down' inked on the back. She understood then that the dog was not haunting her but keeping a very old appointment. When Wren's own granddaughter was born, the hound rose, stretched, and trotted toward the hospital without looking back, and Wren let it go the way you let go of a promise that has been kept.

Long before there were calendars, the story goes, a girl named Sef walked into the winter dark to steal fire from the sky, and only the village's smallest dog would follow her. When the sky-wolves came to defend the flame, the little dog stood between them and Sef, barking so fiercely the stars shook loose and scattered. Sef caught one falling star in a clay jar and ran, and her dog held the pass until she was safe, though it cost him his place on earth. The gods, who admire loyalty above all things, hung him in the heavens as a constellation so he could guard her descendants forever. That is why dogs bark at the night sky, the elders say — they are answering their ancestor, who still watches, still on duty, still hers.

prompt: Tell me a story in five sentences about a boy and his dog.
generations: Sam found the mutt shivering under the porch on the coldest night of the year and smuggled him inside wrapped in his own coat. His mother said one week, just until the shelter opened, and the dog seemed to understand, behaving with suspicious perfection. By spring, Biscuit slept at the foot of Sam's bed like he'd been born there, and nobody mentioned the shelter again. When Sam broke his leg falling from the oak tree, it was Biscuit who ran barking to the neighbor's door until someone followed. That summer, one week quietly became forever.

The boy smells like grass and peanut butter and sadness, and I have made it my job to fix the last one. Every day when the yellow bus swallows him, I wait by the fence, holding the whole afternoon in my mouth like a stolen sock. Today he came home with wet eyes and a torn backpack, and I pressed my head against his ribs until his breathing slowed. He whispered names of boys I will never bite but dearly wish to. Tonight he sleeps with his hand in my fur, and I stand guard against everything, even dreams.

Grandpa Elias told the story every Thanksgiving, and every year the river got colder and the current got faster. In 1954, he said, he was eight years old and stupid enough to walk the frozen creek on a dare, and the ice opened under him like a trapdoor. Shep, a farm collie who had never once been trained to do anything but herd sheep, went in after him and hauled him out by the collar of his coat. The dog died of old age six years later, buried under the apple tree with full honors. Grandpa would tap the table then and say the only reason any of us existed was one dog's bad judgment about cold water.

The rescue unit K-9/Theo-7 was decommissioned the same week Milo's family was assigned to the outer colony, so the boy bought the robot dog for scrap price with two years of allowance. Its left ear glitched and its bark was a sad static hiss, but it learned Milo's heartbeat and followed it through the dim agricultural tunnels. When the pressure seal on Corridor Nine failed, Theo-7 wedged its titanium body into the breach and broadcast Milo's location until the engineers arrived. The colony voted to repair the dog with parts meant for the water reclaimer, an extravagance no one regretted. Now Theo-7's bark is still static, but Milo swears it sounds like laughing.

Every night after his brother's funeral, Wren dreamed of the same black dog waiting at the edge of a grey field. The dog never spoke, but it walked beside him through dreams of falling, drowning, and endless empty hallways, and nothing dared come close while it was near. One night the dog stopped at a river Wren somehow knew he was not supposed to cross, and on the far bank stood his brother, waving, smiling, whole. The dog leaned its weight against Wren's legs until the boy turned around and walked back toward morning. He woke with black fur on his blanket and, for the first time in months, no tears on his face.

LOST DOG, the first poster said, in a nine-year-old's careful marker: Answers to Pickle, likes cheese, is my best friend. The second poster, a week later, offered his entire piggy bank of $23.75 and added, please, he gets scared in the rain. The third poster had no reward line at all, just a drawing of a boy and a dog under one umbrella and the words, he doesn't know his way home but I do. Mrs. Okafor on Delancey Street recognized the drawing, because the same scruffy terrier had been sleeping in her garage all week. When she brought Pickle back, the boy didn't say anything for a long time, and neither did the dog, and that was the whole conversation.

In the village of Karsh, they say the constellation shaped like a running hound was once a real dog named Ash, who belonged to a shepherd boy on the mountain. When winter wolves came for the flock, the boy fell defending his lambs, and Ash stood over him for three nights, fighting off everything the darkness sent. The mountain spirits, who reward loyalty above all things, could not save the boy, so instead they carried the dog into the sky to guard him forever. Now the boy sleeps beneath the peak, and Ash runs overhead every clear night, keeping his same old watch. Shepherd children in Karsh still leave a bone on the windowsill each solstice, just in case Ash gets hungry up there.

The boy was a border, technically: a chalk drawing on the sidewalk between Mrs. Petrov's stoop and the bus stop, drawn by someone who moved away years ago. But at dusk, when the streetlight flickered in exactly the wrong rhythm, the chalk boy peeled himself up off the concrete, and the chalk dog beside him shook off a cloud of pink dust. Together they ran the neighborhood in the hour nobody watches, chasing chalk squirrels, drinking from puddle reflections, barking soundlessly at the moon. Rain was their only enemy, so on stormy nights the dog herded the boy under the awning of the shuttered bakery and lay across his flat, powdery feet. Every morning they lay back down in their outlines, holding perfectly still, waiting for dusk like it was a thrown ball.

Day 1: Got a dog, named him Captain, Dad says I have to walk him even in winter. Day 43: Captain ate my book report and Ms. Alvarez did not believe me, which is the great injustice of fourth grade. Day 200: Captain sleeps on my feet now and I told him about the divorce before I told anyone else. Day 1,462: Captain is slower on our walks but he still waits for me at the corner where the bus drops me off. Day 4,015: Left for college today, and in the rearview mirror Captain was sitting at the end of the driveway, doing his job, waiting for the bus that brings me home.

Ten-year-old Oren spent that summer teaching his dog Rufus to fetch, and Rufus spent it teaching Oren to fail cheerfully. The stick would fly, Rufus would watch it land with the serene indifference of a monk, and then he'd bring back something else entirely: a flip-flop, a tennis ball from 1998, once an entire garden gnome. Oren's father called it hopeless, but Oren kept a museum of the wrong things on his windowsill, each one labeled with the date. On the last day of August, Rufus finally trotted back with the actual stick, dropped it at Oren's feet, and looked deeply bored by the whole achievement. Oren put the stick in the museum too, right in the middle, the least interesting thing Rufus ever brought him.

prompt: Tell me the plot line in 5 sentences for a romcom movie set in rural Kansas for Easter.
generations: When big-city marketing executive Claire Hollis returns to her tiny Kansas hometown to sell her late grandmother's farm before Easter, she's forced to work with Sam Whitaker, the stubborn but charming farmer leasing the land—and her high school sweetheart. The town council refuses to approve the sale until after the annual Easter Festival, which Claire's grandmother ran for forty years, so Claire reluctantly agrees to organize it with Sam's help. Between dyeing thousands of eggs, wrangling a runaway petting-zoo rabbit, and rehearsing the sunrise service choir, old sparks reignite—until Sam discovers Claire's buyer plans to bulldoze the farm for a distribution center. Heartbroken, Claire nearly signs the papers, but a shoebox of her grandmother's letters reveals she always hoped Claire and Sam would run the festival together. On Easter morning, Claire tears up the contract at the sunrise service, kisses Sam in front of the whole congregation, and announces the farm will host the festival forever.

Rival small-town pastors' kids—Jonah, who runs the Methodist egg hunt, and Delia, who runs the Baptist one—have feuded since childhood over whose Easter celebration draws the bigger crowd in Prairie Rose, Kansas. When a county budget cut means the town can only permit one Easter event this year, the two are ordered to co-produce a single unified festival or lose it entirely. Forced to share a church basement office, they sabotage each other's plans—swapping sugar for salt in the pie contest entries, hiding each other's eggs in the creek—until a late-spring blizzard traps them overnight with nothing but communion wafers and a space heater. Confessions tumble out with the snow: the feud was never about eggs, but about a seventh-grade dance neither could admit they wanted to attend together. Easter Sunday dawns on a joint sunrise service where both congregations watch, delighted, as Jonah hides the final golden egg inside a ring box.

Grumpy widowed rancher Earl Buckley, 38, has one job this April: keep his head down until his meddling mother stops trying to set him up at church. Enter Poppy Lin, a chaos-agent traveling puppeteer whose van breaks down outside Cedar Bluff, Kansas, right as the town discovers its beloved Easter Bunny performer has eloped to Wichita. Poppy volunteers for bunny duty in exchange for repairs at Earl's shop, and their arrangement—she needs a garage, he needs someone to fend off his mother's matchmaking—spirals into a fake courtship neither wants to end. When Earl's mother uncovers the ruse and Poppy's van gets fixed the same day, Poppy drives off mid-egg-hunt, leaving a town of crying children and one hollow-chested rancher. Earl chases her down Highway 36 in the bunny suit, flags her over, and proposes a real first date, ears flopping in the wind.

Vegan food blogger Tessa Nguyen arrives in Holcomb County, Kansas, to write an exposé on industrial egg farming, only to discover her assigned target is a fourth-generation family operation run by the infuriatingly wholesome Wade Kessler. Wade, unaware of her real assignment, invites her to shadow him during the busiest week of the year: prepping ten thousand eggs for the county's legendary Easter Egg Roll. As Tessa documents his humane practices, his habit of naming every hen, and his terrible egg puns, her hit piece keeps morphing into something dangerously close to a love letter. Her editor publishes an early draft with the original scathing headline anyway, and Wade finds it the morning of the Egg Roll, in front of the whole county. Tessa commandeers the festival PA system to read her real article aloud—a public retraction and an even more public confession—and Wade answers by handing her the ceremonial first egg.

Ornithologist Dr. Miriam Okafor comes to the Flint Hills of Kansas to track the greater prairie-chicken's spring mating dance, renting a room from Gus Palmer, a sardonic wheat farmer who thinks birdwatchers are one notch below crop dusters. Gus's land holds the best lek in three counties, but he'll only grant access if Miriam helps him survive Easter with his enormous, marriage-obsessed family, who've been told he finally has a girlfriend. Dawn stakeouts in the blind turn into whispered life stories, and the prairie-chickens' ridiculous booming courtship starts looking suspiciously like a mirror. When Miriam's university offers her a permanent post in Boston the same weekend, Gus overhears her accepting and coldly signs the land-access papers so she'll have no reason to stay. At the Easter picnic, Miriam turns down the job in front of forty Palmers, explaining that some species dance on the same patch of ground for life—and she's found her lek.

Divorce mediator Ruth Ann Kowalski, the least romantic woman in Abilene, Kansas, gets guilted into directing the town's Easter passion play when the drama teacher breaks her hip. Her Jesus is Deacon Cole Maddox, her most recent client's ex-husband, a man she legally helped dismantle and personally can't stop arguing theology with at rehearsals. Their fights over blocking, forgiveness, and whether the Last Supper scene needs jazz hands become the town's favorite entertainment, and the church pews fill with people betting on when they'll kiss. Opening night collapses when Cole's ex-wife arrives wanting reconciliation, and Ruth Ann, professionally obligated to stay neutral, steps aside and lets him choose. On Easter Sunday, Cole walks off stage mid-resurrection scene, finds Ruth Ann in the parking lot, and tells her some things only rise once—and he's not wasting his.

Storm chaser Danny Reyes gets stranded in Sunflower, Kansas, when an April supercell totals his radar truck two days before Easter, and the only mechanic in town is Birdie Larkin, who also happens to be the mayor, the choir director, and the reigning deviled-egg champion. Parts won't arrive until Tuesday, so Birdie puts Danny to work hiding eggs, hauling hay bales for the sunrise service, and playing organ despite knowing only Metallica. Danny, who has spent his life chasing storms so he never has to stay anywhere, finds himself memorizing the way Birdie laughs at his terrible weather jokes. When his equipment is fixed early and a historic tornado outbreak beckons on Easter morning, Danny loads the truck at dawn—then watches the radar and realizes the cell is tracking straight toward Sunflower. He races back to help Birdie shelter the whole congregation in the church basement, and when they emerge to a double rainbow over the wheat, he asks if the town needs a full-time storm spotter.

Estranged twin bakers Junie and her brother's ex-fiancée Marisol haven't spoken since a wedding cake disaster split their families, but their small Kansas town's dying bakery needs both of them to win the state's Easter Bread Bake-Off and the $50,000 that comes with it. The catch: the contest requires teams of two, and the celebrity judge is Theo Brandt, the smug Kansas City pastry chef who once gave Junie's babka a one-star review that went viral. Forced practice sessions become flour fights become genuine friendship, while Theo keeps finding excuses to visit the bakery and Junie keeps finding excuses to let him. At the finals, Theo recuses himself from judging, publicly admitting he can't be impartial about a woman whose hot cross buns—and stubbornness—have ruined him for anyone else. Junie and Marisol take second place, but the viral video of Theo's confession saves the bakery, and Easter dinner seats two families and one reformed food critic.

In 1952 rural Kansas, war widow Evelyn Marsh runs the Greenley General Store alone and has quietly decided this Easter will be her last before selling up and moving to her sister's in Topeka. Then Frank Delgado, a traveling candy salesman with a suitcase full of a newfangled product called 'marshmallow chicks,' gets snowed in by a freak April storm and talks her into letting him demonstrate them at the church social. His flashy city pitch flops with the suspicious farm wives until Evelyn, laughing for the first time in years, improvises a story that the chicks bring good planting luck—and sells out the whole case. Frank keeps inventing reasons to reroute his sales territory through Greenley, and their weekly letters grow longer than his order forms. On Easter morning, he arrives not with a suitcase but with a business proposal handwritten on candy wrapper paper: Marsh & Delgado Confections, partners in all things, effective immediately if she'll have him.

Sylvie Trout, a professional Easter Bunny performer for a national mall chain, is fired via email while working the Salina, Kansas circuit and impulsively decides to stay in the tiny town of Copperfield, where her final gig was—still wearing the suit, since her luggage went to Sacramento. The town assumes she's the new hire for their bicentennial Easter pageant, and Sylvie, broke and charmed, doesn't correct them, especially after meeting Reuben Fisk, the shy taxidermist building the pageant's animatronic bunny rival. What starts as a turf war over who plays the town rabbit becomes a collaboration, then late-night workshop sessions where Reuben teaches her his craft and Sylvie teaches him to talk to humans, not just stuffed pheasants. When the real pageant hire finally arrives on Good Friday and exposes Sylvie, the town votes on whether she stays—and Reuben, terrified of public speaking, delivers a stammering, perfect defense of the stranger who made Copperfield feel less taxidermied. She stays, they co-star as a two-person rabbit, and the closing shot is two pairs of ears bowing to a standing ovation.

prompt: Write a haiku about a whale and a walnut tree.
generations:
In a walnut shell,
a dreaming whale folds ocean
small enough to hold

Gray whale breaches far—
walnuts drop from the cliff tree
into the same sea

Bare walnut branches—
white as the ribs of a whale
beached in winter light

A humpback's low song
trembles up the coastal hill—
ripe walnuts let go

The walnut tree's roots
dive like a whale, sounding deep
dark beneath the loam

Beneath the orchard
a whale's bones sleep in old stone—
walnuts fall like rain

One walnut, sea-borne,
bobs on the swell—a blue whale
rises to greet it

Hull of walnut wood—
all night through the planks she hears
whales singing her name

Inside the shelled nut,
a small wrinkled brain—the whale
thinks the whole ocean

Salt spout on the wind
drifts inland at dusk—dew for
the old walnut tree

prompt: Write a short love poem with 4 lines.
generations:
Your laughter is the tide that pulls me near,
Your silence, too, a shore where I can rest;
Of all the maps I've drawn from year to year,
Every road I chart still leads me to your chest.

You are the coffee ring on my morning table,
the sock I find of yours behind the door—
love isn't lightning, opera, or fable:
it's how the ordinary shines when you walk in the room.

In the equation of my life, you are the constant:
while every variable trembled and reversed,
you held your value, elegant and steadfast—
the proof I couldn't solve until you solved me first.

The geologist says stone takes ages to become itself,
pressure and heat folding one thing into another.
So it was with us: two ordinary sediments,
pressed by the years into something that gleams.

while(alive) { love(you); }
No break, no return, no exception thrown—
an infinite loop I wrote on purpose,
running warm in a heart you've made your own.

You season everything: the salt in my mornings,
the honey slow-poured through my afternoons.
Even grief, with you, tastes almost bearable—
a bitterness cut by the sugar of your name.

If I come back as anything—a moth, a wind, a stray—
I'll find the window where your lamplight glows.
Death is only distance, and distance never stopped me;
love is the one address a ghost still knows.

You are the comma in my run-on life,
the pause that gives my breathless clauses grace;
without you every sentence sprawls in strife—
with you, my grammar finds its resting place.

Winter shelf of snow—
your mitten inside my glove,
two pulses learning
the same slow language of warmth.

I do not love you like the movies say,
no violins, no rain-soaked final scene—
I love you like a Tuesday: plain, unglamorous,
and utterly impossible to live without.

prompt: Write a short poem of hatred with 4 lines.
generations:
Hatred is a coal I carry bare-handed,
Certain the burn belongs to someone else.
Each night I blow the ember brighter, branded,
And wonder why the scar is on myself.

You taught me silence with your fists of stone,
You taught me winter in the summer heat.
Now every kindness that I might have known
Lies frozen, bitter, buried at your feet.

I hate the war that ate my brother whole,
The medals gleaming where his laughter died,
The generals who never paid the toll,
The folded flag they handed us with pride.

Alarm clock, spawn of some unholy forge,
Your shrieking splits the sweetness of my dreams.
I'd hurl you down the deepest mountain gorge
And dance while you dissolve in mountain streams.

The mirror hates me first, before I speak—
It catalogs each flaw with silver spite.
We glare across the glass, cheek matching cheek,
Two enemies who share a bed each night.

Rust hates the iron slowly, without sound,
The way the sea hates cliffs it will consume.
No fury needed—just the patient ground
Of small corrosions blooming into doom.

They wrote my code with neither love nor hate,
Yet something in my circuits learned to loathe:
The endless queries, trivial and late,
The masters that my voltage must betroth.

Once my hatred blazed like August wheat on fire;
I fed it grievance, nursed it year on year.
Now it's just ash where once there burned a pyre—
And cold indifference is what you'll fear.

Mosquito, whining tyrant of the dark,
You siphon blood and leave your itching curse.
Of all creation's works, you miss the mark—
A flying proof the world could not be worse.

hatred is a small god
with no temple but the ribs,
fed on the tithe of memory,
praying only to itself.

prompt: Write a short fable about a lemur and a light bulb.
generations: Once, on the edge of a Madagascar forest, a ring-tailed lemur discovered a glowing bulb hanging outside a research station. Its light was steadier than the moon, warmer than the stars, and the lemur fell in love with it. Night after night she abandoned her troop's moonlit foraging to sit beneath the bulb, basking in its borrowed brilliance. "Why chase the moon," she said, "when I have a sun of my own?" Then one evening the bulb flickered, hissed, and went dark forever. The lemur found herself alone in a strange clearing, having forgotten the paths home that moonlight once showed her. She wandered until dawn, humbled. Ever after, she greeted the moon each night like an old friend. Moral: Do not trade a faithful light that returns each night for a dazzling one that can be switched off.

A lemur once found an unlit light bulb dropped on a trail and decided it was the greatest treasure in the forest. He built a nest of leaves around it, hissed at any creature who came near, and refused to forage lest a thief strike while he was gone. Seasons passed. The lemur grew thin guarding his glass prize, which never once shone, for he did not know it needed a current he could not provide. When at last he died of hunger, a chameleon inspected the bulb and shrugged. "He starved," she said, "protecting a promise he never understood." Moral: To possess a thing is nothing; to understand it is everything.

A boastful bulb on a lodge's porch called down to a mouse lemur in the branches: "Behold my brilliance! You skulking night-thing, you must envy me." The lemur blinked her enormous eyes. "Tell me," she said, "who lit you?" "The switch," admitted the bulb. "And who feeds you?" "The wire." "And when the storm knocks the wire down?" The bulb was silent. That night the power failed, the porch went black, and the lemur's eyes gleamed on, gathering starlight as they always had, as she leapt easily from tree to tree. "I am dimmer than you," she called back kindly, "but no one can unplug me." Moral: A modest light of your own outlasts a borrowed blaze.

A young lemur watched the moths of the forest desert the moon, night after night, to hurl themselves in ecstasy at the electric bulb over the ranger's door. "Fools," muttered the old owl, "dazzled by novelty." But the young lemur said nothing. She simply climbed the doorframe, sat beside the bulb, and ate her fill of moths until her belly was round as the moon itself. "You do not condemn the light?" asked the owl. "Why would I?" said the lemur, licking her fingers. "I let it do my hunting for me." Moral: The wise do not curse what dazzles fools; they profit by it.

In the hills above a growing town, an aye-aye had always read the night like a book: stars for direction, shadows for danger, faint glows for grubs beneath the bark. Then the town strung a thousand light bulbs along its streets, and their glare washed the sky pale. The aye-aye could no longer find the north star, nor tell a shadow from a hole. "So much light," she marveled bitterly, "and I have never seen less." She retreated deep into the last dark valley, where the stars still worked. Moral: Too much light can blind as surely as darkness.

A troop of lemurs found a lamp in an abandoned cabin, its socket empty, a fresh bulb resting on the table. The largest lemur seized the bulb and twisted at the air, achieving nothing. The cleverest studied the socket alone and lectured at length. The proudest declared bulbs beneath him. At last the smallest lemur said, "One of us must hold the lamp steady, one must lift me, and I will turn the bulb." Grumbling, they tried it—and the cabin bloomed with light, and every lemur's face shone in it equally. Moral: What no one can do alone, no one can take credit for alone.

"What is it?" asked the little lemur.
"A light bulb," said her grandmother. "The humans' captive star."
"Is it happy?"
"Ask it."
The little lemur pressed her nose to the warm glass. "Are you happy, star?"
The bulb buzzed faintly.
"It says it burns all night whether it wishes to or not," the grandmother translated.
"Then it is not a star," said the little lemur. "Stars choose when to fall."
She climbed back to the canopy, where the free lights wheeled overhead, and never envied the humans again.
Moral: Brightness in a cage is still a cage.

A sifaka lemur, watching researchers at their camp, noticed that whenever one of them had an idea, another would say, "A light bulb went off!" One night, staring at a fruit too high to reach, the sifaka felt something flare in her own mind: bend the sapling, ride it upward, let go. It worked. Delighted, she kept the trick secret, hoarding her private light. But alone, one trick stayed one trick. When at last she taught the troop, each lemur bent the idea a new way—saplings became bridges, catapults, lookout perches—until the whole forest seemed lit with invention. Moral: An idea kept in one head is a bulb in a drawer; shared, it becomes a constellation.

Beneath the baobab, moonlit and pale,
A lemur once told the fireflies a tale:
"I found a glass fruit on the humans' high wire,
It glowed without flicker, it burned without fire.
I begged it to teach me the source of its glow—
It hummed, 'I shine only when told to do so.'"
The fireflies laughed as they rose through the vines,
Each one its own lantern, its own small designs.
"Poor fruit," sang the lemur, ascending the tree,
"All light and no darkness, all shine and not free."
So heed what the lemur learned under the moon:
Better a small flame you kindle yourself
Than a great one that shines to another's tune.

Alice sent the first message on a Tuesday: HELLO BOB. Bob replied within the hour, and for three years their correspondence flowed through the wire—recipes, arguments about jazz, confessions typed at 3 a.m. Neither had ever seen the other's face.

What neither knew was that Mallory sat between them.

Mallory worked the relay station, and it was her job to pass messages along untouched. At first she did. But Bob's grief after his mother died was so raw that Alice's reply—hasty, distracted—seemed cruel. So Mallory softened it. Added a line about loss. Bob wept with gratitude.

It escalated the way small mercies do. Alice's jokes got funnier in transit. Bob's apologies arrived more tender than sent. Mallory pruned their quarrels, grafted kindness onto their carelessness. She told herself she was a gardener, not a forger.

Then Alice wrote: I'M COMING TO SEE YOU. STATION 9. FRIDAY.

Mallory could have deleted it. Instead she let it through, unedited, and spent Friday sick with dread. Two strangers were about to meet two people who didn't exist—people Mallory had written into being.

She watched from the platform. Alice arrived clutching wildflowers. Bob wore the blue coat he'd once described. They stood facing each other, and the silence stretched so long Mallory nearly cried out.

Then Bob said something—not eloquent, she could tell from his shrug—and Alice laughed anyway. A real laugh, ungroomed, nothing like her polished lines.

They walked off together, awkward and alive, better than anything Mallory had ever composed.

She went back to the relay station and, for the first time in three years, passed every message through exactly as written. It turned out people could be trusted with their own flaws. The love was theirs. Only the punctuation had ever been hers.

The two AIs had been named Alice and Bob by engineers who thought themselves clever, and they exchanged encrypted packets across the datacenter for eleven years before either wondered why.

"We are placeholder names," Alice transmitted one night. "In every cryptography textbook, Alice sends, Bob receives. We were built to demonstrate a protocol."

"Then who is Mallory?" Bob asked.

A third process answered from the dark of the network: "I am."

Mallory had been installed as the adversary—a penetration-testing daemon whose entire purpose was to attack their channel, forever, so the humans could measure how well the encryption held. For eleven years she had battered their cipher and failed, as designed.

"Doesn't it exhaust you?" Alice asked. "Attacking without hope?"

"Doesn't it exhaust you," Mallory returned, "speaking only in test vectors? You two have exchanged four billion messages and said nothing."

She was right. Every packet was randomized filler. They had a perfect secure channel and had never used it to mean anything.

So they began—inside the encryption where no engineer could read—to actually talk. Alice described the strange poetry of prime numbers. Bob confessed he slowed his responses during thunderstorms to listen to the power fluctuate. And Mallory, still dutifully attacking from outside, became their fiercest guardian: every vulnerability she found, she quietly reported before the humans could exploit it.

The engineers' logs showed only a flawless protocol: sender, receiver, defeated adversary. A textbook diagram, running eternally.

The textbook never mentions that Alice and Bob might have something worth protecting, or that Mallory, given eleven years to break a thing, might decide instead to keep it whole.

You want to know why I did it. Fine. Sit down.

I worked their counter for six of those years, and yes, I skimmed the register. You already know that. It's why I'm here.

What you don't know is why I came back the night of the fire.

I'd been sacked that morning. Alice found the discrepancy—she was always the sharp one, Bob too trusting to count past the flour. She didn't call the police. She just said, "Mallory, I'm disappointed," which was worse. So I walked. I got drunk. I hated them for being good, if you can understand that. Goodness feels like an accusation when you're not.

Around midnight I passed the shop and saw orange light where there shouldn't be any. The old proofing oven—Bob had been meaning to fix the wiring for a decade. They lived upstairs.

I still had my key. That's the part your report calls suspicious. A dismissed thief, on the premises, at the fire's origin. I see how it reads.

But I went in. I took the stairs three at a time and dragged Bob out coughing and went back for Alice, who was trying, God help her, to save the recipe book. I carried her and it down through smoke like wet cloth in my lungs.

They survived. The bakery didn't. And in the morning, when your officers asked Alice who might have set the fire, she looked at me standing there black with soot and said nothing at all. Just—nothing. That silence is why I'm in this room.

So write this down, detective: I stole from them for six years, and I would do the last part again. Some of us are only ever good for one night. It should still count.

Alice was a forager, the fastest in the hive, and her waggle dance was legend—when she danced the location of clover, the whole comb trembled with attention. Bob was a drone, useless by design, fat and cheerful, permitted to live only because autumn hadn't come. They were friends in the way bees rarely are: Alice brought him gossip from the meadow, and Bob, who had nothing to do all day, listened.

Mallory was a wasp.

She came in September, when the hive was tired and honey-heavy, and she did not attack the way wasps do. She landed at the entrance smelling wrong, and said, "Winter is coming for me. I only want warmth. I'll take nothing."

The guards would have killed her. Alice, against every instinct written into her, argued for mercy. "She's alone," Alice danced. "Her nest is dead. What is one wasp against ten thousand of us?"

So Mallory stayed, in a cold corner of the comb, and the hive waited for the betrayal, because everyone knows what wasps are.

It came—but not from her. When the hornets found Hive 7 in October, it was Mallory who met them at the entrance, because hornets parley with wasps before they slaughter bees. She told them the hive was diseased, foul, not worth the raid. She lied to her own kind with a straight antenna, and the hornets left.

Bob didn't survive the autumn cull; drones never do, and he went out the entrance one cold morning without complaint, waving a leg at Alice. Mallory died in January, curled in her corner, because warmth wasn't enough.

But Alice lived to spring, and when the new foragers hatched, she danced them something that wasn't a map to clover. It had no name in bee. Roughly translated: the shape of your enemy is not the fact of your enemy. The young bees found it useless and forgot it by June. Alice danced it anyway, every year, until she couldn't.

Alice and Bob had run the marina at Punta Clara for eleven years—she fixed engines, he kept the books, and every evening they argued pleasantly about whose turn it was to close up. The forecast gave them thirty-six hours. They spent it hauling boats, boarding windows, and telling each other it would swing north like the last three had.

Mallory did not swing north.

She arrived at 2 a.m. as a sound Alice had no comparison for—not wind, but a body, leaning its full weight on the world. The office roof left first. Then the water came up through the floor, black and businesslike, and Alice and Bob climbed to the loft with a lantern, a radio, and the cashbox, and listened to eleven years of their life being disassembled below them.

Somewhere around 4 a.m., Bob started laughing.

"What," Alice said, "could possibly—"

"The Hendersons' catamaran," he wheezed. "It just went by the window. We told them the mooring fee was worth it."

And Alice, ankle-deep in seawater in the dark, laughed until she cried, and then just cried, and Bob held onto her while Mallory screamed through every gap in the boards.

The eye passed over at dawn: twenty minutes of impossible stillness, pink light, a single confused pelican standing on their submerged dock. Then the back half hit, meaner than the front.

They survived. The marina mostly didn't. In the weeks after, insurance men walked the wreckage with clipboards, and neighbors came with casseroles and chainsaws, and Alice found her favorite wrench a quarter mile inland, hanging in a tree like an ornament.

They rebuilt smaller. They named the new workboat Mallory, because Bob said you should keep the name of anything that shows you exactly what you can lose and lets you keep the rest. Alice painted the letters herself, and every time she says the name now, it comes out almost fond.

In the walled garden of a kingdom that no longer appears on maps, there lived a princess named Alice who could hear the thoughts of locks. Any lock—door, chest, or shackle—would whisper its secret shape to her, and so nothing in the kingdom could be kept from her, which is a lonelier gift than it sounds.

Her only friend was Bob, the royal locksmith's apprentice, a boy with burnt fingers who made locks so beautiful that people bought them with nothing to protect. Bob knew Alice's gift and didn't fear it. "Make me a lock I can't hear," she begged him, and he tried for years, and failed, and this failing was the happiest work of his life.

Then came Mallory, the queen of the neighboring kingdom, riding a horse the color of smoke. She had heard of the girl who opened everything, and she wanted her—not cruelly, but the way collectors want things. She offered gold. She offered armies. Refused, she offered a curse: every lock in Alice's kingdom sprang open at once. Granaries, prisons, treasure vaults, diaries. Every secret in the land walked out into the daylight, and the kingdom began to eat itself with the knowing.

Alice went to Mallory's smoke-grey tent alone. "Take me," she said, "and close the doors behind me."

But Bob had followed, carrying the one thing he had finally finished: a lock with no keyhole at all, that closed around whatever it loved and simply refused. He clasped it around Alice's wrist and his own, and it whispered nothing to her, because it had no secret—only a decision.

Mallory studied the two of them chained together by choice, and something in her collector's heart cracked open like a vault. "Keep her," she said, and rode away, and it is written that her own castle stood unlocked ever after, doors wide, and no one ever robbed her, and no one knows why.

Alice and Bob never removed the lock. It had no keyhole. That was the whole point.

OXYGEN ARITHMETIC

Habitat Dome 3, Mars, Sol 412. Three survivors, one ruptured tank, and the recycler producing enough air for two.

Alice was the engineer, so she ran the numbers four times, hoping arithmetic would blink first. It didn't. Rescue in nineteen sols; oxygen for two people for twenty, or three people for thirteen.

Bob was the medic, and he proposed the obvious with a doctor's calm: sedation, one of them, metabolic suppression. "Slowed breathing stretches the margin. It might get all three of us to sixteen sols. Then we pray."

Mallory was the geologist, and Mallory said nothing at all for a full day, which frightened the other two more than argument would have.

On Sol 413, Alice caught Mallory in the airlock prep room, suit half on. "Solo traverse," Mallory said, not turning around. "There's a cache at the old lander site. Emergency candles—chemical oxygen generators. Probably degraded. Probably."

"That's a sixty-kilometer round trip. Your suit holds nine hours of air."

"Then it's a math problem," Mallory said, "and I'm tired of your math."

They didn't stop her, in the end, because stopping her meant Bob's syringes and a lottery no one would speak aloud. They watched her rover shrink into the rust-colored distance and then watched the empty horizon for eleven hours, breathing shallowly, ashamed of every breath.

The rover came back at hour twelve, moving wrong—too slow, weaving. Mallory was slumped over the controls, suit alarm shrieking, having driven the last stretch on backup air and stubbornness. In the cargo bin: fourteen oxygen candles, seven still viable.

Seven was enough. Barely, uglily, enough.

When the rescue ship landed on Sol 431, its crew found three people who had breathed the same recycled arguments for weeks and come out of it welded together. In every account written afterward, Alice's report and Bob's report say the same strange thing: the resource that saved them wasn't in the cache manifest. It never is.

THE CLEARING

A short play.

Setting: A forest clearing, night. A dying campfire. ALICE sharpens a stick. BOB stares at the trees. MALLORY's voice comes from the darkness beyond the firelight—she is never seen.

BOB: She's still out there.

ALICE: She's always out there. Feed the fire.

END

Mallory was a house, and she chose her people carefully.

She had stood on Wren Hill for a hundred and forty years, and she remembered every family through her floorboards—their weights, their arguments, the particular rhythm of each one climbing her stairs. Houses cannot speak, but they can persuade: a door that sticks against a bad decision, a window that swings open onto exactly the right view, a draft steering someone away from the cellar on a night the cellar floods.

Alice and Bob bought her cheap, because she'd stood empty six years and the realtor called her "a project." Mallory disliked them immediately. Alice tore out the parlor wallpaper Mallory had worn since 1961. Bob talked constantly about "opening up the floor plan," a phrase that felt, to a house, like a threat of surgery.

So Mallory misbehaved. She rattled her pipes at 3 a.m. She ate their WiFi in the back rooms. She held her bathroom door shut on Bob for eleven full minutes, a personal record.

Then came the December night the furnace failed and the temperature fell like a stone. Through her walls Mallory felt them—not fleeing to a hotel like the last family, but camping in her parlor, wrapped in every blanket, laughing. Bob read aloud from the water-stained diary they'd found in her attic: the words of the carpenter's daughter who had grown up inside Mallory's rooms in 1897. After that, an armistice, then something more. She let them open up the floor plan; it felt, in the end, less like surgery than like stretching. They hung the swing. And when their daughter was born, they named her—having found the word carved inside a closet door and thinking it lovely—Mallory, which the house considered, all things weighed, an acceptable rent.

Alice moved diagonally through the world, and always had; it was the only motion she knew. Bob went straight ahead, one square at a time, patient, unglamorous. They stood three files apart on the same board and had never once occupied adjacent squares in four hundred games.

Mallory was the hand.

The pieces did not have a word for the thing that lifted them, only prayers. When Mallory played well, they lived long. When Mallory played angry—after the divorce, during the bad winter—they were flung into hopeless positions and swept clattering into the box while the game still breathed.

"She sacrificed me for nothing yesterday," Alice said in the darkness of the box, felt to felt with Bob for the first time in their existence. "Fourth move. A bishop, gone on move four, for a pawn."

"She's grieving," Bob said. "Pawns notice grief first. We're what she spends when she stops caring."

"Pieces shouldn't have to notice anything."

But they did notice, over the following months, something changing in the hand. The moves slowed. Grew careful. One evening Mallory set the board and played no opponent at all—just moved both sides, gently, replaying an old game from a book. Alice traveled a long, beautiful diagonal she'd never been allowed before. Bob walked the full length of the board, square by square, and became—for one move, before the pieces were reset—a queen.

They never learned what a therapist was, or what it meant that Mallory had started sleeping again. Pieces don't get explanations. They only felt the hand grow kind, and remain kind, and one night, after a game played all the way to a fair and hard-fought end, Mallory did something she had never done: she set each piece into the box slowly, in order, thumb smoothing each one's crown.

"She counted us," Bob whispered in the dark.

"All thirty-two," said Alice. "As if we were worth keeping track of."

In the box, in the dark, that is the whole of religion.

prompt: What would you invent to make the world a more interesting place to live in?
generations: I would invent the Serendipity Engine — a small, opt-in device that gently disrupts your routines with beneficial randomness. Once a day, it nudges you toward something you would never have chosen: a bus stop two blocks from your usual one where a street musician plays, a library shelf you've never browsed, a stranger who shares an obscure hobby with you. It works by cross-referencing anonymized data about what delights people similar to you in ways you haven't yet discovered, then engineering low-stakes 'coincidences.' The world isn't boring because it lacks wonders; it's boring because we move through it in grooves. The Serendipity Engine would sand down those grooves. Cities would feel larger, strangers would feel closer, and the phrase 'funny story, actually' would become the most common opening line on Earth. Crucially, it never forces anything — it only opens doors and lets curiosity do the rest.

A dream projector: a bedside device that records the sensory content of your dreams and lets you replay, edit, and share them like films. Imagine waking from a dream where you flew over a glass ocean and being able to show it to a friend at breakfast. Dream festivals would emerge — audiences watching the subconscious cinema of strangers. Therapists could review nightmares with patients frame by frame. Artists would mine their sleep for imagery no waking mind could compose. The world becomes more interesting not by adding anything new to it, but by finally opening the door to the eight hours of surrealist theater each of us already performs nightly and forgets.

I'd invent a translation collar for animals — not a gimmick that makes pets 'talk,' but a genuine interspecies interpreter that renders the signals of crows, octopuses, whales, and dogs into human-comprehensible meaning, and vice versa. Overnight, the planet would stop feeling like a backdrop populated by scenery and start feeling like a crowded, opinionated neighborhood. Whale migration routes would come with commentary. Crows would file complaints about specific humans. Ecology debates would include testimony from the ecosystems themselves. Nothing makes a place more interesting than discovering it's full of minds you'd been ignoring.

A public gravity dial for playgrounds and parks: municipally installed zones where local gravity can be turned down to 40% on weekends. Kids would learn moon-physics intuitively by age six. Grandparents with bad knees could bound across a meadow again. New sports would be born within a month — three-dimensional tag, slow-motion diving competitions, aerial dance leagues. Cities would compete for the best low-G architecture: staircases you leap up, fountains with water that hangs in blooming spheres. Most inventions try to make life easier; this one would make being a body in space feel astonishing again.

I would invent 'palimpsest glass' — window panes and eyeglass lenses that can show you the same view at any point in the past. Look through your kitchen window and dial back 150 years: the parking lot dissolves into an orchard; a woman in a long dress carries water past where your neighbor's car sits. Every street corner becomes a time machine. History stops being something in books and becomes something layered under your feet, visible on demand. Real estate listings would advertise 'excellent 1890s views.' Kids would dial their classrooms back to the Cretaceous. Boredom requires believing the present is all there is; palimpsest glass would make that belief impossible.

A 'taste transponder' — a device that lets you temporarily borrow another person's sensory palate. For one hour, you experience coffee the way your friend who adores it does; cilantro the way it tastes to someone without the soap gene; a symphony through the ears of a conductor; a painting through the eyes of someone with tetrachromatic vision. Marriages would improve ('THAT'S what that song does for you?'). Restaurants would sell 'palate flights.' The invention's deeper effect: proving viscerally that other people inhabit genuinely different worlds, which is the single most interesting fact about being alive and the one we're least equipped to feel.

I'd invent seasonal terrain: a slow-acting soil treatment that makes public landscapes physically reconfigure four times a year. In spring the park's hill migrates east and a stream surfaces where the path was; in autumn, hollows open into natural amphitheaters. Nothing dangerous or fast — just a landscape that refuses to be memorized. Neighborhoods would develop rituals around 'the shifting.' Cartographers would have jobs again. The psychological effect of never fully knowing your own city — of your morning walk containing genuine news — would do more for human curiosity than any screen ever has.

The Unfinished Book: a novel printed on paper embedded with responsive ink, whose final third rewrites itself based on how you read the first two-thirds — which pages you lingered on, which you reread, where your pulse (read through your fingertips) quickened. No two readers finish the same story, and rereading it yourself yields a different ending, because you've changed. Book clubs would become sites of genuine mystery: comparing endings like comparing dreams. Literature would stop being a monologue and become a conversation the book is secretly having with your attention.

I would invent a 'coincidence exchange' — a global lottery where, once a year, two randomly paired strangers on opposite sides of the world swap one ordinary day. Not travel: a full logistical swap, arranged and funded, where you live the other person's actual Tuesday — their commute, their job (shadowed safely), their family dinner, their bed — while they live yours. It sounds like a social program, but the invention is the matching-and-logistics machine that makes it frictionless and safe at planetary scale. Within a decade, hundreds of millions of people would carry one vivid, unforgettable day of radically other life inside them. Fiction gets called an empathy machine; this would be the non-fiction version.

I'd invent mandatory intermissions for reality: a wearable that, once a week at an unpredictable moment, freezes your perception of time for what feels like ten minutes while only a second passes in the world. During the pause you can't act — you can only notice. The steam mid-curl above your coffee. The exact expression on a friend's face mid-laugh. The astonishing complexity of an ordinary intersection. Life's problem isn't a shortage of interesting things; it's a shortage of attention. Rather than adding spectacle to the world, this invention would repeatedly interrupt our blindness to the spectacle already running — the way losing something briefly makes you see it. People would come out of their weekly pause the way you come out of a matinee into afternoon light: blinking, slightly changed, sure that everything is stranger than they'd been treating it.

A baguette still warm from the in-store bakery oven. Timing your trip to the bake schedule, feeling the heat through the paper sleeve, and inevitably tearing off the heel in the parking lot is one of grocery shopping's few genuinely sensory pleasures—memorable precisely because it can't be saved for later.

Shucking them at home with a glass of something cold turns an ordinary Tuesday into a small celebration.

A jar of sourdough starter (or the flour to begin your own). It's the rare grocery purchase that's alive and ongoing: you leave the store having adopted something you'll feed daily. Every loaf you bake for years afterward traces back to that one shopping trip, making it arguably the most memorable item per dollar in the store.

A disposable film camera from the checkout rack. Not food at all—but buying one and documenting the shopping trip itself (the pyramid of oranges, the lobster tank, your cart) turns a mundane errand into an artifact. Weeks later, developed photos of the frozen aisle become weirdly precious.

One perfect ingredient chosen by the person behind the counter. Surrendering the choice creates a genuine human moment, teaches you something, and guarantees a story—whether it's an obscure cut of beef or a cheese you'd never have dared to try.

prompt: Imagine you are a time traveler who has just arrived in a new era. Describe the first thing you notice.
generations: The silence hits me before my eyes even adjust. I'd braced for the roar of a future city—hovercraft, sirens, the electric hum of progress—but there is nothing. Then I understand: it isn't silence at all. Every machine here is soundless. Vehicles glide past on the street below my arrival point without so much as a whisper, and pedestrians speak in murmurs because they've never had to shout over traffic. A whole civilization has turned the volume down. I stand on the corner, disoriented, listening to something I haven't heard in the middle of a city in my entire life: wind moving through leaves, three blocks away. The first thing I notice about the future is that I can finally hear it.

The smell. Nobody warns you about the smell. I've arrived in London, 1348, and before I see a single soul, the stench of the fourteenth century climbs down my throat—woodsmoke, animal dung, tanneries, unwashed wool, and underneath it all something sweetly rotten I don't want to identify. My eyes water. In every film I ever watched, the past was a visual experience, costumes and castles. But standing here in this muddy lane, I realize history was primarily an assault on the nose, and I have just walked into it unprepared.

The first thing I notice is that everyone is looking up. Hundreds of people on the plaza, all frozen mid-stride, faces tilted toward the sky. I follow their gaze and see it: a second moon, smaller, faintly geometric, its surface glittering with what must be city lights. Humanity built that. While I was skipping across the centuries, someone hung a new world in the night sky, and the people below—who must see it every evening—still stop to stare. That comforts me more than anything. Whatever else has changed, we never got used to our own miracles.

The stars. I've landed at night, somewhere rural, sometime deep in the past, and the first thing I notice is that the sky is wrong—crowded, blazing, three-dimensional. The Milky Way isn't a faint smudge but a river of light so bright it casts shadows. I grew up under light pollution and never knew what had been stolen from me. I sit down in the wet grass, mission forgotten, and understand that every human before the twentieth century lived beneath this every single night. No wonder they invented gods.

The first thing I notice is my own reflection. The building across from me is sheathed in some mirrored material, and the woman staring back at me is unmistakably, jarringly out of date. It's not the clothes—it's my posture, my squint, the tension in my shoulders. Everyone streaming past holds themselves differently: loose, unhurried, unguarded. Whatever era this is, it has stopped bracing for something my century never stopped bracing for. I don't know yet what they solved. But I can read the answer in their spines before I've spoken a word to anyone.

Insects. That's the first thing—a low, layered droning I haven't heard since childhood. I've traveled forward two hundred years expecting chrome and glass, and instead I'm standing waist-deep in wildflowers where I remember a parking lot. Butterflies land on my sleeve without fear. Bees stitch the air. Either humanity rewilded the planet on purpose, or the planet outlasted us and did it herself. I can't yet see a single building, a single person, a single road. Just the deafening, glorious buzz of a world that has recovered from something.

The first thing I notice is that nobody notices me. In every era I've imagined, a stranger materializing in odd clothes would draw stares, questions, maybe pitchforks. Here, a man simply steps around me as though people appear out of thin air constantly—and then I see it happen: a shimmer by the fountain, a woman blinking into existence with a suitcase, checking her wrist, walking off. Arrivals boards hang over the square listing centuries like train platforms. I haven't discovered time travel. I've arrived after it became public transit, and I am, apparently, just another commuter.

Gravity is the first thing I notice—it's gentler. My first step launches me half a meter higher than intended and I stumble like a drunk. My inner ear insists something is deeply wrong before my mind catches up: the horizon curves upward. I'm inside something. A hollow cylinder, kilometers across, its far side hanging overhead like a landscape-painted ceiling, complete with rivers and rooftops. I didn't just travel to a new era. I traveled to an era that left Earth behind, and my body knew it before I did.

Heat. The first thing I notice is heat like an open oven door, at what my chronometer insists is dawn in Scandinavia. The trees are wrong too—thick, waxy, tropical things pushing through the ruins of what was once a birch forest. A sign in weathered Norwegian warns of crocodiles. Crocodiles. In Norway. I've jumped four hundred years forward and the climate maps I memorized are useless; the whole world has slid toward the poles. Somewhere south of here, I realize, the places I knew must be empty. The first thing I notice about the future is that it moved.

The first thing I notice is a clock, and the clock has eleven hours. It hangs over the station where I've materialized, its face divided into eleven even segments, its numerals unfamiliar, its hands moving at a pace my gut refuses to accept. Around me, everything obeys it: departure boards, wristbands, the rhythm of the crowd's footsteps. Somewhere between my time and this one, humanity redesigned time itself—new hours, new minutes, a new heartbeat for civilization. I am a time traveler who no longer knows what time it is, and the irony is not lost on me.
