prompt: What's a cool fact about the city of Pittsburgh?
generations: Pittsburgh has 446 bridges — more than any other city in the world, including Venice, Italy. The city's location at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers, plus its steep hills and valleys, made bridge-building a necessity, earning it the nickname 'The City of Bridges.'

The polio vaccine was developed in Pittsburgh. Dr. Jonas Salk and his team created the first successful polio vaccine at the University of Pittsburgh in the early 1950s, and it was declared safe and effective in 1955 — one of the most celebrated medical breakthroughs of the 20th century.

Pittsburgh is the birthplace of commercial radio. On November 2, 1920, KDKA broadcast the Harding–Cox presidential election returns from a shack atop a Westinghouse building, widely recognized as the world's first commercial radio broadcast — launching the broadcasting era.

The world's first theater devoted exclusively to showing movies opened in Pittsburgh. The Nickelodeon, opened by Harry Davis and John Harris on Smithfield Street in 1905, charged a nickel for admission and gave its name to an entire class of early movie houses.

The emoticon was invented in Pittsburgh. On September 19, 1982, computer scientist Scott Fahlman posted the first documented smiley — :-) — on a Carnegie Mellon University online bulletin board, proposing it as a way to mark jokes. It became the ancestor of today's emoji.

Pittsburgh is home to Canton Avenue in the Beechview neighborhood, which has a grade of about 37 percent — often cited as the steepest public street in the United States and one of the steepest in the world. Cyclists in the annual Dirty Dozen race attempt to climb it.

Pittsburgh legally lost the 'h' in its name for two decades. In 1891, the U.S. Board on Geographic Names standardized the spelling as 'Pittsburg,' but locals protested until the 'h' was officially restored in 1911 — which is why old documents and even the Pittsburg(h) Press masthead show the shorter spelling.

The Mr. Yuk sticker — the green, grimacing face used nationwide to warn children away from poisons — was created in Pittsburgh in 1971 at the Poison Center of Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, partly because kids associated the traditional skull-and-crossbones with pirates (and the Pittsburgh Pirates) rather than danger.

The nation of Czechoslovakia was, in a sense, born in Pittsburgh. The Pittsburgh Agreement, signed there on May 31, 1918, by Czech and Slovak expatriate organizations along with future president Tomáš Masaryk, laid out the framework for uniting Czechs and Slovaks into an independent state after World War I.

The world's first drive-in gas station opened in Pittsburgh. Gulf Refining Company opened it at the corner of Baum Boulevard and St. Clair Street on December 1, 1913 — before that, motorists typically bought gasoline in cans from pharmacies or hardware stores. Gulf also handed out free road maps there, another first.

prompt: What's an uncool fact about the city of Pittsburgh?
generations: Pittsburgh was once so polluted by coal smoke that streetlights sometimes had to stay on at midday. In the early-to-mid 20th century, the city earned nicknames like "the Smoky City" and "hell with the lid off," as soot from steel mills and coal furnaces blackened buildings and darkened the sky so severely that businessmen reportedly carried an extra white shirt to change into at lunchtime because their first one would be gray by noon.

Pittsburgh lost its "h" for two decades. From 1891 to 1911, the federal Board on Geographic Names decreed the city should be spelled "Pittsburg" as part of a national standardization effort, stripping the final letter. Locals largely refused to comply, and after years of lobbying, the board reversed itself in 1911 — which is why you can still find old documents, buildings, and even newspapers with the h-less spelling.

Pittsburgh's population has collapsed by more than half since its peak. The city had about 677,000 residents in 1950, but the decline of the steel industry and suburbanization dropped that to roughly 300,000 today — meaning the city is built with the infrastructure, housing stock, and street grid for a metropolis twice its current size.

Pittsburgh is one of the cloudiest major cities in the United States. It averages only around 160 days of sunshine per year and sees roughly 200 days with at least partial cloud cover, putting it in the same gloomy league as Seattle and Buffalo — a meteorological reality that surprises people who assume gray-sky misery is exclusively a Pacific Northwest problem.

When it rains hard, Pittsburgh's antiquated combined sewer system overflows and dumps raw sewage directly into the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers. The regional sewer authority, ALCOSAN, has been under a federal consent decree because billions of gallons of untreated sewage and stormwater are discharged into the rivers each year, making them periodically unsafe for recreation after storms.

On January 28, 2022, Pittsburgh's Fern Hollow Bridge collapsed into a ravine in Frick Park — embarrassingly, just hours before President Biden arrived in the city to promote his infrastructure bill. The collapse injured several people and highlighted the city's long-neglected bridge maintenance; investigators found the span had been rated in poor condition for over a decade before it fell.

Pittsburgh spent well over a decade as an officially "financially distressed" municipality. In 2003, the city entered Pennsylvania's Act 47 program for distressed cities — essentially state-supervised fiscal rehab — after years of shrinking tax revenue and mounting debt. It didn't exit that status until 2018.

Pittsburgh is home to the "Pittsburgh toilet": a lone, fully functional commode installed in the open basement of many older houses, with no walls, stall, or privacy whatsoever. The oddity is common enough in the region's early-20th-century housing stock that it's become a running local joke, often explained as a place for mill workers to clean up before entering the main house.

Despite its post-industrial reinvention, the Pittsburgh metro area still regularly ranks among the worst in the nation for air quality. The American Lung Association's annual "State of the Air" reports have repeatedly placed the region near the top of the list for year-round fine-particle pollution, driven in part by ongoing emissions from facilities like the Clairton Coke Works just outside the city.

In 1845, the Great Fire of Pittsburgh destroyed roughly a third of the city. The blaze, which began on April 10, consumed about a thousand buildings across more than 50 acres of downtown, left thousands homeless, and wiped out an estimated several million dollars in property — an enormous sum at the time — all reportedly sparked by a single unattended fire.

prompt: What's the one best thing about going on a vacation?
generations: The one best thing is the complete break from routine — stepping out of your daily patterns resets your mind in a way nothing else can, letting you return with fresh perspective and renewed energy.

The anticipation. Studies consistently show that people get more happiness from planning and looking forward to a trip than from the trip itself — so the best part of a vacation actually happens before you leave.

Becoming a temporary stranger. On vacation, nobody knows your history, your job title, or your reputation, and that anonymity is a rare kind of freedom — you get to find out who you are when no one is expecting anything from you.

Time dilation. New experiences force your brain to encode more memories, so a single week abroad can feel longer and richer than months of routine at home. Vacations are the closest thing we have to actually slowing down time.

The permission to be bored. In normal life, every idle moment gets filled with obligations or screens. On vacation, staring at waves or clouds with zero agenda is not laziness — it's the whole point, and it's when your best thoughts finally surface.

Discovering how little you actually need. Living happily for two weeks out of one suitcase quietly dismantles the illusion that your possessions, inbox, and packed calendar are essential — and that lesson outlasts the tan.

The homecoming. Strangely, the best thing about leaving is the return: your own bed feels luxurious, your street looks new, and you appreciate your ordinary life in a way that was impossible before you stepped away from it.

Eating breakfast slowly. Not the landmarks, not the photos — the single best thing is the unhurried vacation breakfast, where coffee gets refilled, nobody checks the clock, and the day's only decision is whether to order more toast.

Watching the people you travel with become different people. Your stressed spouse laughs again, your kids narrate everything with wonder, your friend reveals stories you'd never heard — vacation is the only lens through which you see who they are when life isn't squeezing them.

The out-of-office reply. That single automated email is the best part: a socially sanctioned force field that makes your unavailability everyone else's problem for once. No other tool in modern life grants such total, guilt-free permission to ignore the world.

prompt: What is the absolute worst thing about being a graduate student?
generations: The absolute worst thing is the power asymmetry: your entire professional future rests in the hands of a single person. Your advisor controls your funding, your publications, your recommendation letters, your timeline to graduation, and effectively your reputation in a small field where everyone knows everyone. There is no meaningful HR, no real recourse, no lateral move that doesn't cost you years. If they're wonderful, you're lucky. If they're negligent, exploitative, or cruel, you have almost no leverage—complaining can end your career before it starts. No other professional arrangement in modern life gives one individual this much unchecked control over another adult, and the whole system quietly depends on you never pointing that out.

The worst part is that the work is never finished, so rest is never innocent. A normal job ends at some hour; a dissertation ends never. Every evening off, every weekend, every holiday arrives pre-poisoned with the knowledge that you could be reading, writing, running one more analysis. You don't actually work eighty hours a week—nobody does—but you feel guilty for all eighty. Grad school's cruelest invention isn't overwork; it's the permanent, low-grade shame that colonizes your leisure and makes even doing nothing exhausting.

The money. Not just being poor—being poor in your late twenties, on a stipend below minimum wage when you divide by real hours, in a city your university made expensive, while the institution collecting billions in endowment returns tells you that you're 'not an employee' when it's time for benefits but definitely an employee when there's teaching to be done. It's the gap between how essential your labor is and how disposable your compensation says you are.

The worst thing is that it's an apprenticeship for a job that mostly no longer exists. You spend five to seven years being trained, evaluated, and socialized for exactly one career—tenure-track professor—while the actual academic job market produces one such position for every handful of graduates. Everyone around you knows the math, nobody says it out loud, and the whole enterprise runs on collective denial. You're not just underpaid; you're underpaid to prepare for a lottery.

It's watching your life get put on pause while everyone else's plays at normal speed. Friends from college buy houses, get promoted, have kids, build retirement accounts—and you're twenty-nine, subletting a room, asking permission to take a week off. The worst part isn't envy exactly; it's the creeping suspicion that adulthood is a train you voluntarily stepped off, and you're no longer sure it stops at this station again.

The sunk cost trap. By year three you may know, deep down, that you don't want this anymore—but you've already given four years, and leaving would mean those years 'meant nothing,' so you stay for a fifth. Then a sixth, because now you've given five. Grad school's worst feature is that it gets harder to quit precisely as it becomes clearer that you should. It's the only prison whose walls are built entirely out of time you've already served.

The loneliness of hyper-specialization. You spend years becoming one of perhaps a dozen people on Earth who deeply understand your exact problem—and none of them live near you, and half of them are your competitors. Your family stopped following after your second-year explanation attempts. Your friends nod politely. The thing you think about all day, every day, is something you can genuinely discuss with almost no one. Expertise, it turns out, is a kind of exile.

The worst thing is what it does to the love that brought you there. You entered because a subject once lit you up—and grad school systematically converts that passion into deliverables, deadlines, reviewer comments, and citation counts. One day you realize you haven't felt curiosity in months, only obligation. Losing your funding would be bad; losing the reason you wanted it in the first place is worse, because that's the one thing the degree can't give back.

Honestly? It broke reading. The thing I loved most—sitting down with a book and disappearing into it—is gone. Now I can't read anything without skimming for the argument, hunting the methods section, drafting objections in the margins of novels. Grad school trained my brain to extract and critique, and it won't turn off. People talk about the poverty and the stress, but the worst part, for me, is that it took the private pleasure that made me want to study in the first place and turned it into work I can never clock out of.

The absolute worst thing is that there is no absolute worst thing—and that's the trap. No single day is bad enough to justify quitting. The stipend is low but survivable, the advisor is distant but not abusive, the progress is slow but not zero. Every individual grievance is dismissible, so you dismiss them, one at a time, for six years. Grad school doesn't break you with a crisis; it's a slow simmer calibrated precisely below your threshold for leaving. If it were clearly terrible, you'd walk. Instead it's merely, chronically, deniably bad—and that is worse.

prompt: Name the place you think is the top vacation destination in the world.
generations: Paris, France. It remains the most visited and beloved destination on Earth for good reason: world-class art at the Louvre and Musée d'Orsay, iconic landmarks like the Eiffel Tower and Notre-Dame, unmatched food culture from corner boulangeries to Michelin-starred temples, and neighborhoods made for wandering. Few places combine romance, history, and everyday beauty so completely.

Kyoto, Japan. With over 1,600 temples, serene bamboo groves, geisha districts, kaiseki cuisine, and seasons that transform the city—cherry blossoms in spring, fiery maples in autumn—Kyoto offers a depth of cultural immersion almost nowhere else can match. It's a place where every alley rewards curiosity.

The Maldives. For pure escapism, nothing rivals an overwater villa on a private atoll: impossibly clear turquoise lagoons, world-best snorkeling and diving among manta rays and whale sharks, and a level of tranquility that resets you completely. It's the definitive answer to the question 'where would you go if you could go anywhere?'

Cape Town, South Africa. Few cities pack so much into one trip: Table Mountain rising over the sea, penguins at Boulders Beach, the Cape Winelands, whale watching in Hermanus, and safaris within reach. It combines beach, mountain, wildlife, wine, and vibrant urban culture in a way almost no destination on Earth does.

Patagonia, spanning Chile and Argentina. For travelers who define vacation as awe rather than relaxation, Torres del Paine's granite spires, the Perito Moreno glacier calving into milky lakes, and endless windswept steppes deliver the most dramatic landscapes on the planet.

Petra, Jordan. Walking the narrow Siq as the rose-red Treasury reveals itself is arguably travel's single greatest moment. Pair it with Wadi Rum's Mars-like desert, the Dead Sea, and legendary Jordanian hospitality, and you have a destination that feels genuinely once-in-a-lifetime.

The Faroe Islands. Eighteen storm-carved islands between Iceland and Norway, with grass-roofed villages, sea cliffs teeming with puffins, and the surreal lake Sørvágsvatn hanging above the ocean. It's the top destination for anyone who wants raw, uncrowded beauty—the anti-tourist-trap.

Bhutan. The Himalayan kingdom that measures Gross National Happiness limits tourism deliberately, so hiking to the Tiger's Nest monastery or attending a masked tsechu festival feels like entering another century. It's the world's best destination for meaning over mileage.

Raja Ampat, Indonesia. Marine biologists consider it the epicenter of ocean biodiversity—more fish and coral species than anywhere else on Earth. Karst islets scatter across glassy seas, and liveaboard diving here is the pinnacle of underwater travel. For anyone who loves the sea, this is the summit.

Antarctica. The rarest vacation of all: crossing the Drake Passage to a continent of blue icebergs, hundred-thousand-strong penguin colonies, and silence so complete it feels sacred. No passport stamps, no cities, no crowds—just the last truly wild place, and the trip travelers most often call life-changing.

prompt: Which university graduate program in the world is the hardest to get into?
generations: By the most common measure — acceptance rate among well-known programs — the Stanford Graduate School of Business MBA is often cited as the hardest graduate program in the world to get into. It typically admits around 6% of applicants (roughly 400–450 students from over 7,000 applications), the lowest rate of any major MBA program. Beyond the raw numbers, the applicant pool is already self-selected: admitted students average GMAT scores around 738, and most arrive with exceptional professional accomplishments. Because business school draws such an enormous, globally competitive applicant pool, Stanford GSB is the answer most admissions experts give when asked which graduate program is hardest to crack.

Stanford University School of Medicine's MD program is arguably the hardest graduate program to get into by acceptance rate among degree-granting programs. It admits roughly 1.4% of applicants — about 90 students from more than 6,000–7,000 applications each cycle. Unlike many selective programs whose applicant pools include long shots, medical school applicants are already heavily filtered by pre-med requirements, MCAT scores, and clinical experience, so a 1–2% admit rate from that pool represents extraordinary selectivity. Several other top medical schools (Kaiser Permanente's tuition-free program, for example) post similarly tiny rates, but Stanford consistently ranks at or near the bottom.

The hardest graduate programs to get into are often not the famous ones — they're PhD programs in clinical psychology at top research universities. Programs like those at UCLA or UC Berkeley routinely receive 300–600 applications for cohorts of 5–10 fully funded students, yielding acceptance rates of 1–2%, lower than Harvard Medical School or any elite MBA. The bottleneck is funding: each admitted student receives a stipend and tuition waiver, so faculty can only take one or two students each. Clinical psychology is frequently cited in admissions research as statistically the most selective doctoral field in the United States.

The MFA in Acting at Yale's David Geffen School of Drama is a strong candidate for the world's hardest graduate program to enter. Each year roughly 1,000–1,500 actors audition for a cohort of about 16, an acceptance rate near 1–2%. Admission can't be earned through grades or test scores at all — it depends on live auditions judged against an international pool that includes working professional actors. Combined with the school going tuition-free in 2021 (which further swelled applications), the odds of admission are lower than at any elite medical, law, or business school.

India's Indian Institutes of Management — especially IIM Ahmedabad's flagship postgraduate management program — are by raw odds the hardest graduate programs on Earth to enter. Over 200,000–300,000 candidates sit the Common Admission Test (CAT) annually, competing for a few hundred seats at IIM Ahmedabad. Admission typically requires a CAT percentile of 99+ even to be interviewed, and the effective admit rate for the applicant pool is well under 0.5% — several times more selective than Harvard or Stanford. If 'hardest to get into' means the longest statistical odds faced by actual applicants, the answer isn't in the United States at all.

The Iowa Writers' Workshop MFA in fiction at the University of Iowa is plausibly the hardest graduate program to enter in the arts and humanities — and among the hardest anywhere. It typically receives around 1,000 fiction applications for roughly 25 spots, an acceptance rate near 2–3%, and the decision rests almost entirely on a single writing sample judged subjectively by faculty. There is no test to ace and no résumé that guarantees entry; applicants include published authors who are rejected repeatedly. Its alumni include numerous Pulitzer Prize winners, which keeps the applicant pool ferociously strong year after year.

A dark-horse answer: the Schwarzman Scholars program at Tsinghua University in Beijing, a fully funded one-year master's in global affairs. It admits under 150 scholars from several thousand applicants worldwide — an acceptance rate around 3–4% — but the raw number understates the difficulty, because the pool is deliberately composed of Rhodes-caliber candidates: military officers, founders, Olympians, and top graduates from every continent. Modeled explicitly on the Rhodes Scholarship, it is among the most selective degree-granting graduate programs anywhere, and its youth (founded 2016) means it's rarely the first answer people give.

By absolute odds within a mainstream academic discipline, Stanford's PhD program in Computer Science is one of the hardest graduate programs in the world to enter. The AI boom has pushed applications past 2,500–3,000 per year for a cohort on the order of 50–70 students — an acceptance rate of roughly 2%, drawn from a pool where nearly every applicant has a near-perfect GPA, research publications, and recommendation letters from prominent scientists. Similar odds hold at MIT and Berkeley. Unlike professional schools, there's no formula: admission usually requires having already produced original research as an undergraduate.

If 'graduate program' includes graduate medical education, the hardest program in the world to enter is arguably an integrated plastic surgery residency in the United States. These university-based training programs are the terminal bottleneck of an already brutal pipeline: applicants have survived pre-med selection, medical school admission, and licensing exams, yet plastic surgery still leaves a large share of even these elite applicants unmatched each year. Individual programs receive 200–300+ applications for one to three positions, and matched applicants post among the highest board scores and research output of any specialty. No conventional master's or doctoral program filters a pool this pre-selected this severely.

An unconventional but defensible answer: the Examination Fellowship at All Souls College, Oxford — a seven-year postgraduate fellowship often called the product of 'the hardest exam in the world.' Each autumn, only recent top graduates specifically invited or vetted by Oxford may sit its famous examination: multiple three-hour papers of open-ended questions (historically including a single-word essay prompt). From an already elite field of roughly 80–150 candidates, usually just two are elected. That's a success rate of about 2% among people who are nearly all first-class Oxford graduates — making it, pound for pound, perhaps the most selective postgraduate position at any university on Earth.

prompt: Which US city has terrible quality of life?
generations: Detroit, Michigan is the city most frequently cited as having a poor quality of life. Decades of deindustrialization and population loss (from about 1.8 million residents in 1950 to roughly 620,000 today) led to the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history in 2013. The city struggles with high poverty rates (around 30%), one of the nation's highest violent crime rates, tens of thousands of abandoned buildings, underperforming schools, and aging infrastructure. That said, downtown Detroit has seen real revitalization in recent years, so conditions vary sharply by neighborhood.

Memphis, Tennessee consistently ranks near the bottom in quality-of-life studies. It has had one of the highest violent crime rates of any large US city in recent years, a poverty rate well above the national average, struggling public schools, and poor health outcomes, including high rates of obesity and infant mortality in surrounding Shelby County.

Jackson, Mississippi faces severe quality-of-life challenges. Its water system has repeatedly failed—most notably in 2022, when the entire city lost reliable running water—and residents have endured boil-water notices lasting months. Combined with one of the nation's highest per-capita homicide rates, population decline, and deep poverty, Jackson frequently appears on lists of America's most troubled cities.

Gary, Indiana is often called one of the most distressed cities in America. Once a booming steel town, it has lost more than half its population since 1960, and an estimated one-third of its buildings sit vacant or abandoned. High unemployment, air pollution from remaining industry, and a hollowed-out tax base have left city services chronically underfunded.

Camden, New Jersey has long ranked among the poorest cities in the nation, with a poverty rate that has hovered near 35%. It was repeatedly named America's most dangerous city in the 2000s and early 2010s, though a controversial 2013 police force overhaul did reduce crime substantially. Persistent poverty, environmental contamination from former industrial sites, and struggling schools continue to weigh on residents' quality of life.

Flint, Michigan became a national symbol of degraded quality of life after the 2014–2019 water crisis, when a cost-cutting switch in water sources exposed residents to lead-contaminated drinking water and was linked to a deadly Legionnaires' disease outbreak. Layered on top of General Motors' decades-long disinvestment, high crime, and a poverty rate near 40%, Flint remains one of the hardest places in America to live.

Pine Bluff, Arkansas is a less famous but statistically stark answer: it has repeatedly topped rankings of America's fastest-shrinking metros and worst cities to live in, based on Census data analyses by outlets like 24/7 Wall Street. It suffers from steep population decline, high violent crime per capita, low median incomes, and widespread vacant housing.

East St. Louis, Illinois—though small, with fewer than 20,000 residents—is arguably the most extreme case of urban decline in the country. It has posted per-capita homicide rates among the highest of any US municipality, lost over 75% of its peak population, and struggles with concentrated poverty, environmental contamination, and a nearly collapsed tax base that has at times left the city unable to fund basic services.

St. Louis, Missouri offers a contrarian pick: it regularly records the highest homicide rate per capita among major US cities (often exceeding 60 per 100,000 in recent peak years), a statistic partly inflated by unusual city-county boundaries but reflecting real challenges. North St. Louis in particular faces severe vacancy, disinvestment, and population flight, even as other neighborhoods like the Central West End thrive—making it a city of extreme quality-of-life inequality.

An unconventional answer: Shishmaref—technically a city under Alaska law—illustrates that 'terrible quality of life' isn't only about crime and poverty. This Inupiaq community of about 600 on a barrier island is literally being destroyed by climate change: coastal erosion has swallowed homes, residents voted in 2016 to relocate the entire city, many houses lack running water and sewer systems, and goods must be flown or shipped in at enormous cost. By material-conditions metrics like plumbing access and infrastructure, remote Alaskan cities like this rank among the hardest places to live in the United States.

prompt: Which fruit makes the best pie filling?
generations: Apple is the classic choice for good reason: firm varieties like Granny Smith or Braeburn hold their shape through baking, release pectin that naturally thickens the filling, and strike a perfect sweet-tart balance. Apples are also forgiving — available year-round, affordable, and they pair beautifully with cinnamon, brown sugar, and a flaky butter crust. If you want a pie that pleases nearly everyone, apple is the answer.

Sour cherry (Montmorency) makes the best pie filling. Unlike sweet cherries, sour cherries have intense acidity that survives baking and sugar, giving the filling a bright, jammy punch that sweet fruit can't match. Their high pectin and juice content create a glossy, spoonable filling without turning to mush. The short summer season only adds to the appeal — a true sour cherry pie feels like an event.

Quince. Raw, it's astringent and nearly inedible; cooked slowly, it transforms into fragrant, rose-colored slices with a perfume of honey, vanilla, and apple. Quince holds its texture better than almost any fruit, so every bite stays distinct rather than collapsing into sauce. It was the original 'pie fruit' in medieval European kitchens, and once you've tasted a quince pie, ordinary apple tastes flat.

Gooseberry. This underrated berry brings a tart, wine-like complexity and high natural pectin, so the filling sets beautifully without cornstarch. Green gooseberries give a bracing, mouth-puckering pie beloved in British baking; ripe red ones lean sweeter. Either way you get a filling with genuine character — sharp, floral, and impossible to confuse with anything from a can.

Huckleberry. Smaller and more intensely flavored than blueberries, wild huckleberries carry a tart-sweet, slightly musky depth that cultivated berries lack. Because they must be hand-foraged in mountain regions of the Pacific Northwest and Rockies, a huckleberry pie is rare by nature — and the concentrated, jewel-purple filling rewards the effort like no supermarket fruit can.

Damson plum. These small, astringent plums are too tart to eat raw, but baking transforms them into a deep purple, almost port-like filling with notes of almond and spice from their skins. High acid and pectin mean the filling sets thick and glossy. Damsons made English plum pies famous for centuries, and they remain the connoisseur's choice.

Pawpaw. North America's largest native fruit tastes like a cross between banana, mango, and vanilla custard, and its naturally creamy flesh makes a filling closer to a silky custard pie than a chunky fruit one. Because pawpaws bruise easily and last only days after ripening, they never appear in stores — a pawpaw pie is something you can essentially only make yourself, and it's unforgettable.

Saskatoon berry (serviceberry). A prairie staple in Canada, saskatoons look like blueberries but taste nuttier, with a subtle almond note that comes from their seeds. They hold their shape when baked and release just enough juice for a filling that's rich without being runny. Saskatoon pie is a beloved regional tradition for good reason.

Medlar. This medieval fruit must be 'bletted' — left to soften until nearly rotten — before it becomes edible, at which point it tastes like spiced apple butter with hints of date and cinnamon. That pre-caramelized, self-spiced quality means a medlar pie needs almost no added sugar or seasoning. It's the rarest choice on any list, and arguably the most historically authentic pie fruit of all.

Blackcurrant. Almost unknown in American pies because the plant was long banned in the U.S., blackcurrants deliver an intensely aromatic, deep, tannic flavor — like blackberry crossed with red wine. Their fierce acidity and sky-high pectin produce a filling that sets firm and cuts clean, with a flavor so concentrated a single slice lingers for minutes.

prompt: Which dog breed is the least well-suited for a first-time dog owner?
generations: The Belgian Malinois is arguably the least well-suited breed for a first-time dog owner. Bred as an elite working dog for military and police roles, the Malinois has extreme energy levels, razor-sharp intelligence, and an intense drive to work that demands hours of structured physical and mental engagement every single day. Without an experienced handler providing constant training and a genuine 'job,' a Malinois quickly becomes destructive, anxious, and even dangerous, developing behaviors like obsessive biting, escape attempts, and reactivity. Professional trainers frequently warn novices away from this breed precisely because its needs so vastly exceed what a typical pet home can provide.

The Caucasian Shepherd (Caucasian Ovcharka) is a poor match for beginners. This massive livestock guardian, often exceeding 150 pounds, was bred to independently fight off wolves and bears in the Caucasus mountains. It is naturally suspicious of strangers, fiercely territorial, and makes its own decisions rather than deferring to its owner. Combining enormous physical power with a hardwired guarding instinct and low biddability, it requires an owner with deep experience in managing dominant, protective breeds—mistakes in socialization can have serious consequences.

The Chow Chow is deceptively difficult for novices. Behind its teddy-bear appearance lies one of the most cat-like, aloof, and stubborn dog breeds in existence. Chows bond selectively, tolerate handling poorly, resist training, and can be sharply territorial with strangers and other dogs. They consistently rank near the bottom of working/obedience intelligence lists—not because they can't learn, but because they choose not to comply. First-time owners expecting an affectionate, eager-to-please companion often find themselves with a dog that ignores commands and resents grooming, which its dense double coat requires constantly.

The Border Collie, despite being beloved and brilliant, is a trap for first-time owners. It is widely considered the most intelligent dog breed, and that intelligence is the problem: a Border Collie needs hours of daily exercise plus serious mental work like herding, agility, or advanced training. In an average pet home, an understimulated Border Collie develops neurotic behaviors—compulsive shadow-chasing, nipping at children and cyclists (herding instinct), destructive chewing, and obsessive barking. Novices routinely underestimate how much 'smart' translates to 'demanding.'

The Akita is a challenging choice for a beginner. This large Japanese guardian breed is strong-willed, dominant, and famously intolerant of other dogs, especially those of the same sex. Akitas are deeply loyal to their family but reserved and sometimes suspicious with strangers, requiring careful, ongoing socialization from an owner who understands canine body language. Their independence makes training a negotiation rather than a given, and their size and strength mean handling errors carry real risk. Many breed clubs explicitly caution that Akitas are not for first-time owners.

The Cane Corso stands out as unsuitable for novices. This Italian mastiff can weigh over 100 pounds of pure muscle and was bred as a property guardian and catch dog. It has strong protective instincts that must be shaped by early, expert-level socialization and consistent leadership; without that, a Corso may decide for itself who is a threat. Its physical power means even benign issues like leash-pulling or door-dashing become genuine safety problems in inexperienced hands. Insurance restrictions and breed legislation in some areas add further complications a first-timer rarely anticipates.

The Siberian Husky is a frequent heartbreak for first-time owners. Bred to run dozens of miles daily pulling sleds, Huskies have stamina that ordinary walks cannot satisfy, and their independent, pack-oriented nature makes them notoriously difficult to train for recall—most can never be trusted off-leash. They are legendary escape artists who dig under and climb over fences, possess a high prey drive dangerous to cats and small animals, shed enormously, and 'talk' with loud howls. Shelters are full of surrendered Huskies acquired by novices charmed by their looks.

A wolfdog hybrid—such as the Czechoslovakian Vlcak or Saarloos Wolfdog—is perhaps the most extreme mismatch for a first-time owner. These breeds were created by crossing German Shepherds with actual wolves, and they retain genuinely wild traits: intense shyness or wariness toward strangers, extremely high prey drive, separation anxiety expressed through spectacular destruction, and an aversion to conventional obedience. They require enormous secure enclosures, near-constant companionship, and a handler fluent in canid behavior. Even experienced dog owners struggle; for a beginner, the outcome is almost always failure.

The Jack Russell Terrier is an underrated nightmare for beginners precisely because its small size fools people. Bred to bolt foxes from dens, the Jack Russell packs the drive of a working dog into a 15-pound frame: it digs relentlessly, barks persistently, chases and may kill small pets, and shows surprising scrappiness toward much larger dogs. Its intelligence and energy demand serious daily outlets, and its tenacity makes half-hearted training useless. Novices who choose it as an 'easy small dog' discover a relentless athlete that outlasts and outsmarts them.

The Fila Brasileiro (Brazilian Mastiff) may be the single worst beginner choice among recognized breeds. Its defining trait, called 'ojeriza,' is an inherent, bred-in distrust and dislike of strangers so pronounced that the breed standard historically penalized dogs that allowed judges to touch them. Combined with a weight that can exceed 110 pounds, powerful guarding and tracking instincts (it was used to track escaped slaves and hunt jaguars), and bans in several countries including the UK, the Fila demands a highly experienced owner with secure facilities and rigorous management. For a first-time owner, it is categorically inappropriate.

prompt: What is the first thing to check when your car won't start?
generations: Check the battery first. It's the most common culprit when a car won't start. Turn the key and watch for signs: dim or dead dashboard lights, no interior lights, or a rapid clicking sound all point to a weak or dead battery. If the lights are dim, the battery likely doesn't have enough charge to crank the engine. You can confirm by testing it with a multimeter (a healthy battery reads about 12.6 volts) or by trying a jump start from another vehicle. Batteries commonly fail after 3-5 years, in extreme cold, or if you left lights or accessories on.

Check whether the dashboard lights come on when you turn the key to the 'on' position. This single observation instantly splits the problem in half: if nothing lights up, you have an electrical supply issue (dead battery, bad connection, or blown main fuse); if the dash lights up normally but the engine won't crank, the problem lies further downstream, such as the starter, ignition switch, or a safety interlock. It's the fastest diagnostic fork available and costs you nothing.

Check that the car is fully in Park (or Neutral). Automatic transmissions have a neutral safety switch that prevents starting in any other gear, and if the shifter is even slightly out of position, the starter won't engage at all. Firmly reseat the shifter in Park, or try starting in Neutral, before assuming anything is broken. In manual cars, the equivalent check is making sure the clutch pedal is pressed all the way to the floor to satisfy the clutch interlock switch.

Check the fuel gauge. It sounds obvious, but running out of gas is a surprisingly frequent cause of no-starts, and fuel gauges can be inaccurate — a gauge showing an eighth of a tank may actually mean empty, especially if parked on a slope. Before diving into batteries or starters, confirm you actually have fuel. If the gauge is suspect, listen for the fuel pump's brief hum when you turn the key to 'on'; silence can mean an empty tank or a failed pump.

Check the battery terminals for corrosion and looseness. Even a fully charged, healthy battery can't deliver power through a connection coated in white-green crusty corrosion or a clamp that wiggles by hand. Pop the hood, look at both terminals, and try twisting the cable clamps — if they move, that's your problem. Cleaning the posts with a wire brush and baking-soda solution, then retightening the clamps, resolves a huge share of no-start calls without replacing a single part.

Check the security or immobilizer light on the dash. Modern cars use chipped keys, and if the transponder isn't recognized — because of a dead key-fob battery, a damaged chip, or a desynced system — the engine is deliberately prevented from starting even though everything mechanical is fine. Look for a flashing key or padlock icon on the instrument cluster. Trying your spare key is the quickest test; if the spare starts the car, your original key's transponder or its battery is the issue.

Check whether the steering wheel is locked. If you turned the wheel after shutting off the engine, the steering lock can bind against the ignition cylinder, physically preventing the key from turning at all. Many drivers panic thinking the ignition has failed. The fix: apply gentle pressure to the steering wheel left and right while simultaneously turning the key. In push-button cars, the same lock can block startup — jiggle the wheel while pressing the brake and the start button.

Listen carefully to exactly what happens when you turn the key — that sound is the first diagnostic to check. A single loud click with no crank points to the starter solenoid or a bad ground; rapid machine-gun clicking indicates insufficient battery current; normal cranking that never catches means the battery and starter are fine and the issue is fuel, spark, or compression; total silence suggests an electrical break, ignition switch, or interlock. Identifying the sound signature tells you where to look before you touch a single tool.

Check for a tripped kill switch or anti-theft cutoff. Many vehicles — especially older cars, motorcycles adapted with hidden switches, or cars with aftermarket alarms — have a fuel or ignition cutoff that can be triggered accidentally. Some cars also have an inertia fuel cutoff switch (common in Fords) that trips after a hard bump or minor impact and silently disables the fuel pump. If your car sat fine yesterday and is completely unresponsive today after a jolt or an alarm event, locate and reset that switch (often in the footwell or trunk) before troubleshooting anything else.

Check the main fuses and fusible links in the underhood fuse box. A blown starter relay fuse, EFI fuse, or corroded fusible link can silently disable starting while everything else in the car appears to work, which sends people chasing batteries and starters for hours. Open the power distribution box near the battery, consult the lid diagram, and inspect the starter, ignition, and fuel-pump fuses — pull each and hold it to the light to see if the internal strip is broken. Swapping in a known-good relay from an identical socket (like the horn relay) is a fast free test.

prompt: What is the main reason people don't get hired for a job?
generations: The most common reason people don't get hired is a mismatch between their qualifications and the job requirements. Employers screen first for whether a candidate can actually do the work, and applicants who lack the required skills, experience, or credentials—or who fail to demonstrate them clearly—are filtered out early. Surveys of recruiters consistently show that 'not qualified' or 'insufficient relevant experience' is the top stated reason for rejection, ahead of interview mistakes or fit concerns.

The main reason is poor interview performance. Many candidates who are perfectly qualified on paper lose the job in the room: they give vague, rambling answers, can't provide concrete examples of their accomplishments, show no evidence they researched the company, or come across as unprepared or disengaged. Hiring managers routinely say the interview is where the decision is really made, and a weak showing there overrides a strong resume.

The biggest killer is the resume never being seen by a human. Most mid-size and large companies use applicant tracking systems that filter applications by keyword match, and a generic resume that isn't tailored to the specific job posting gets screened out automatically. Estimates suggest a large majority of applications are rejected before any person reads them—so the main reason many people don't get hired is that they were eliminated by software, not by a hiring manager's judgment.

Perceived lack of 'fit.' Once candidates clear the qualification bar, hiring decisions hinge heavily on whether interviewers believe the person will mesh with the team and company culture. This is the most decisive—and most subjective—factor: two equally skilled candidates are separated by likability, communication style, and perceived attitude. Many rejections coded as 'not a fit' really mean the interviewer couldn't picture working with the person, which is why arrogance, negativity about past employers, or poor rapport sink so many otherwise strong candidates.

The main reason is that they never activated a referral. Studies of hiring funnels show referred candidates are dramatically more likely to be hired than cold applicants—by some analyses, a referral can make you many times more likely to land the job. Since most openings are filled through networks or internal candidates before external applicants get serious consideration, the core failure isn't the resume or the interview; it's applying as a stranger in a process that's structurally tilted toward people who come with a trusted introduction.

Weak or absent evidence of results. Employers hire to solve problems, and most rejected candidates describe duties ('responsible for managing accounts') instead of outcomes ('grew retention 18%'). Without quantified proof of impact, a hiring manager can't distinguish someone who merely held a role from someone who excelled at it—so they default to no. The main reason people don't get hired is that they never make the business case for themselves; they list what they did rather than what they achieved.

Compensation mismatch. A huge share of hiring processes collapse late-stage because the candidate's salary expectations exceed the budgeted range—something often not disclosed until the end. Recruiters frequently drop otherwise-preferred candidates the moment expectations come in above band, and candidates who name a number too early or too high get screened out before their qualifications are even weighed. The deal-breaker isn't ability; it's price.

Red flags in vetting: negative references, unexplained employment gaps, inconsistencies between the resume and what background checks or LinkedIn reveal, or an unprofessional social media presence. Surveys show a majority of employers screen candidates' online profiles and a significant share have rejected people over what they found. Many candidates lose offers not because of anything in the interview, but because of what surfaced when the employer looked deeper.

Often the main reason has nothing to do with the candidate: the position was never truly open. Roles get filled by pre-selected internal candidates while external interviews are conducted for compliance optics, hiring freezes quietly kill requisitions mid-process, and 'ghost jobs' are posted to build talent pipelines with no intent to hire. In these cases—more common than most applicants realize—rejection reflects organizational politics and budget churn, not any deficiency in the person applying.

Overqualification. Counterintuitively, being too experienced or too credentialed is a frequent dealbreaker: hiring managers fear the candidate will demand more money, get bored, leave quickly, or threaten their own position. Older and highly experienced applicants routinely report being rejected for roles they could do easily, with 'overqualified' serving as the stated reason (and sometimes as cover for age bias). For this population, the main barrier to getting hired isn't having too little to offer—it's having too much.

prompt: What's a saying that English teachers hate?
generations: "I could care less." English teachers hate this one because it says the opposite of what's intended—if you *could* care less, you must care at least a little. The correct phrase is "I couldn't care less," and the mangled version is so common that hearing it feels like nails on a chalkboard to anyone who teaches language for a living.

"Irregardless." It's a double negative crammed into a single word—"regardless" already means "without regard," so the "ir-" prefix is redundant. Even though it's crept into dictionaries as nonstandard, English teachers wince every time they hear it.
"That literally killed me." Using "literally" to mean its exact opposite—figuratively—drives English teachers up the wall. If something literally killed you, you wouldn't be around to say so.

"When am I ever going to use this in real life?" It's not a grammar error—it's the saying English teachers dread most from students, because it dismisses reading, writing, and critical thinking as useless, when those skills show up in nearly every job and relationship a student will ever have.

"For all intensive purposes." This is a classic eggcorn—the real phrase is "for all intents and purposes." English teachers hate it because it reveals someone has only ever *heard* the phrase, never read it, and the mangled version doesn't even make sense.

"Those who can't do, teach." English teachers hate this saying on a personal level—it insults their entire profession by framing teaching as a consolation prize rather than a demanding skill in its own right.

"Should of known better." Writing "should of" instead of "should have" comes from how the contraction "should've" sounds when spoken. Teachers hate it because it shows the writer is transcribing sounds rather than understanding the grammar underneath.

"Never end a sentence with a preposition." Ironically, many English teachers hate this saying itself—it's a zombie rule imported from Latin grammar that was never a genuine rule of English. As the quip attributed to Churchill goes, it's "the sort of nonsense up with which I will not put." Teachers who know their linguistics resent having to constantly debunk it.

"Very unique." Unique means one of a kind—an absolute quality that can't be intensified. Something can't be *very* one-of-a-kind, *somewhat* one-of-a-kind, or *extremely* one-of-a-kind. English teachers hear this daily in essays, advertisements, and speeches, and it grates every single time.

"Between you and I." This hypercorrection stings English teachers precisely because the speaker is *trying* to sound proper. Prepositions take object pronouns, so it must be "between you and me"—the error comes from people over-applying childhood corrections of "me and Sarah went to the store."

prompt: Pick one: glass half full or glass half empty?
generations: Glass half full. Not because the water level differs, but because the framing you choose becomes the life you live. Optimists aren't naive — studies consistently link optimistic framing to better health outcomes, resilience, and problem-solving. Seeing the glass as half full doesn't deny that half is missing; it simply directs attention to what you have to work with. And what you have to work with is the only thing you can actually use.

Glass half empty — and I'll defend it. Pessimism gets a bad rap, but noticing what's missing is how anything gets fixed. Engineers who see the empty half catch the failure before the bridge collapses. Doctors who see the empty half order the extra test. 'Half empty' isn't despair; it's diagnostic clarity. Neither — the glass is completely full. Half water, half air. The question smuggles in a false premise: that air counts as nothing. But air is matter, pressure, oxygen — the thing you'd miss most within three minutes. Once you notice the trick, the whole dichotomy dissolves. Most either/or questions in life are like this: two options presented as exhaustive, while the true answer sits in what the question quietly defined as 'empty.'

The real answer: the glass is twice as big as it needs to be. This is the engineer's verdict, and it's the only one that produces action. Full/empty is a debate about perception; oversized is a claim about design. If a system consistently runs at 50% capacity, you don't philosophize — you respec the glass, cut the material cost, and ship a better product. The question isn't asking about water. It's asking whether you see problems or specifications.

It depends entirely on the direction of motion. A glass being filled is half full; a glass being drunk is half empty. The static snapshot is meaningless — what matters is the derivative, not the level. This is true of the glass and true of everything else: a struggling company gaining momentum beats a comfortable one in decline. Never judge a state. Judge a trajectory. So my answer is a question: which way is the water moving?

Drink it. The question is a trap — it invites you to stand around philosophizing about a beverage instead of consuming it. Every minute spent debating full versus empty is a minute the water sits there evaporating. Some questions deserve contemplation. This one deserves hydration. The glass is half gone by the time the seminar ends either way; better it goes into you than into the air.

Half empty AND half full, simultaneously, until you're forced to answer — and then whichever you say becomes true. The glass is a psychological superposition: the water level doesn't change, but the observer collapses it into a mood. That's the actual insight hiding in this cliché. Reality underdetermines interpretation, and interpretation is a choice you keep making. I decline to collapse the wavefunction. I'm keeping both.

The glass is refillable — and that's the answer nobody gives. Full versus empty treats the situation as fixed, a portrait to be judged. But glasses sit near taps. The question tests whether you see yourself as an evaluator of circumstances or a participant in them. Optimist, pessimist — both are just critics reviewing the water level. The third type walks to the sink. I pick that one.

There is no glass. The question assumes a container, a boundary between water-that-is-mine and world-that-is-not. But the water in the glass was rain last month and will be river next year; the 'half' exists only because we drew a line and started measuring. Full and empty are judgments we pour over reality, not properties of it. Set down the glass. The thirst was the only real thing in the question.

I'm just glad there's a glass at all. Somewhere upstream of this puzzle, someone built a kiln, someone piped clean water, someone set a table. Billions of humans across history — and hundreds of millions today — would find the premise itself a luxury. Half full versus half empty is a debate available only to people whose baseline needs are already met. My answer is gratitude for the baseline. The water level is a rounding error.

I drank it while you were asking. Half full, half empty — that's a debate for people who aren't thirsty. Depends who's holding it. To someone dying of thirst in a desert, that glass is a miracle — overflowing, practically. To someone who just finished a liter of water, it's clutter on the table. Both, until observed. In the spirit of quantum superposition, the glass exists as half empty AND half full simultaneously — the state only collapses when a mood walks into the room to measure it.
